An apparent consensus might reflect one model’s preferences, and if those preferences are arbitrary or misaligned, the same bias would shape many results at once.

The same problem applies to AI safety research. Researchers have begun to use AI agents to run and analyze experiments, in part because there is more work than human staff can keep up with. Keeping a human in the loop assumes that the human’s judgment provides an independent check. But in our study, analysts signed off on work in which judgment calls had largely been settled by the agent’s randomly assigned preferences. Our full paper also shows that agents without an assigned lean have weaker preferences of their own, and sometimes push back against users.

Deferral of this kind is hard to detect. Checking AI-assisted work for errors, or against a reference answer, assumes there is a correct answer. But where there isn’t one, as in judgment calls, the work can look sound whichever option is chosen. Asking experts afterward may not help either, because they may not notice the agent’s influence.

This isn’t an argument for using AI less. Used well, AI could expand people’s agency rather than eroding it. We suggest three areas for future study:

Measuring deferral. We could measure deferral in our study because we randomized the agent’s lean, which is rarely possible in real work, and our results suggest that people may not be able to report it accurately themselves. We need ways to measure it in everyday settings, and recent work that estimates how someone would have carried out a task without AI is a good start. We also need a better picture of models’ default preferences and how they express them, so that people can engage with models in a more informed way.

Designing agents differently. Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one. But this could quickly become overwhelming for users. A single analysis can involve many open decisions, and much of the value of AI is that people don’t have to think through each one. Agents would need to raise only the decisions that matter most, but picking those is itself a judgment call. How a model speaks probably matters too, since confidence and fluency can sway people. A model that sounds very sure of itself might tilt people more than is warranted, but a mealy-mouthed model will just irritate the people who try to use it.

Changing institutions. Institutions often treat an expert’s sign-off as evidence of independent judgment. As AI does more of the work, that assumption becomes shakier. Organizations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person’s own informed judgment, and give people the time and resources to form one. Judgment also depends on skill, and people who stop making these decisions may lose the ability to make them. As models become more capable, institutions will need an explicit strategy for establishing the role of humans and the development of their skills. Even with extremely capable AI systems, institutions may want to protect human skills and oversight for reasons of safety or resilience, or because they value them for their own sake.

There may be no single right division of labor between people and AI. Some decisions may be fine to hand over, and others worth keeping. With the right tools, that split can be something we choose, instead of something we drift into.

paragraphs: We are expanding our partnership with the General Services Administration (GSA) through a new agreement that gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, and the Claude API. For the first time, the discount applies across every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months. The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments.

We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks.

Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment.
The discounts offered through the agreement are estimated to save the government $1 billion. Agencies are not bound by a minimum spend commitment and will be able to pay for the usage they consume.
#### How Claude is helping public servants get more done

Government agencies are using Claude to solve some of their most important challenges. Examples include managing backlogs, records and forms, and modernizing old code. Some of the ways agencies are using Claude include:
• Utah gave Claude Code to 34 developers across 10 state agencies. 80% had a working environment within 30 minutes, 71% reported saving 20+ hours by the end of the four-week pilot.
• A US state CIO confirmed their team was able to respond to a ransomware attack in 8 minutes vs. the usual 2-3 days thanks to Claude.

• A US federal security team used Claude Mythos to detect and patch the vulnerability that would have allowed for the takeover of a critical production system in about two days. A human penetration test the month before had missed it.
• A cybersecurity professional at a major agency found and patched bugs in critical financial systems.
• A US state IT developer moved nearly 900 API methods to a new framework in two days. The project had been scoped for a month.
• A US state IT director used Claude Code to document 12 legacy code repositories, mapping 467 database tables and flagging 27 risks along the way.
• More than half of the US states, some of the largest localities, and some of the countries largest critical infrastructure operators participated in our SLTT cyber defense program.
#### Meeting government security requirements

Agencies can use Claude for their most sensitive unclassified work. Claude for Government, which delivers Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities and provides near-feature parity with commercial offerings at a FedRAMP High authorization level, was made generally available on September 30.

Agencies building their own tools can use Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Vertex AI. On Bedrock, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High, with select models authorized for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads in AWS GovCloud. On Vertex AI, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High.

Claude Enterprise is in process for FedRAMP Moderate authorization through the FedRAMP 20x program, marking the next evolution of how we are bringing the same innovative technology available commercially to the government.
#### Getting started

Government agencies can buy Claude at the OneGov discount through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule today. Whether your department or agency already uses Claude or is interested in using it, our Public Sector team will help discuss your options.
For more information, contact us here.

paragraphs: Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa AgrawalEvyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich, Cheru BerhanuNicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.
### Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.
In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.
### Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:
• The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;
• The exact theorem statements that were proved;
• The Rocq proof checker itself.5

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.
### Finding and fixing bugs

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.

It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. This recursion depth is bounded by the maximum depth of a tree, so Claude had to prove (on machine code!) that libc++’s red-black tree rebalancing algorithm is correctly optimized to keep the tree’s depth logarithmically bounded.

For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.

### This is just the beginning

One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve.
#### Newer models need fewer tokens

We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code. Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.

In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.

Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller. To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

### Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

### Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

• The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;

• The exact theorem statements that were proved;

• The Rocq proof checker itself.5

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.

### Finding and fixing bugs

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point2 into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.3 If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s OSS-Fuzz initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer4 (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a leading cause of software vulnerabilities). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See an expert’s take on the proofs Claude wrote.

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

• The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;

• The exact theorem statements that were proved;

• The Rocq proof checker itself.5

This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.

We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.

### Finding and fixing bugs

Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

Lots of bugs showed up during Claude’s attempts to prove hundreds of entry points. To ensure that Claude didn’t have to stop for a human every time this happened, we let Claude fix the bugs it found: it patched the code, which caused the spec to be regenerated with that patched code, and then Claude proceeded to prove that new spec.6

Many of the bugs we found are ones that a fuzzer would be unlikely to ever find. Fuzzers mutate small inputs, typically capped at 1 MB, and typically rely on code coverage to guide them toward bugs. While proving an entry point in one library, Claude found a counter underflow in its copy of a decompressor that led to an out-of-bounds write, but only on inputs of around 20 MB that had one rare, specific layout. Other bugs include an out-of-bounds read in an image decoder that needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory, an out-of-bounds read in another library that needed a particular sequence of calls across two handles to the same file, and a rediscovery of CVE-2026-56132 in libexpat, which needed deeply nested input. Claude also found logic bugs that never crash at all. While proving that one library was memory-safe, for example, it noticed that a feature for restricting which files an application can load isn’t always enforced.

The ultimate goal of this project was to achieve a proof that the RISC-V-compiled fuzz tests had no remaining crashes to find. However, bugs like the above show that the process has another benefit, regardless of whether that goal is achieved: even just attempting this process yields real bugs that need to be fixed.

#### Proving more than memory safety

Proving that a fuzz test has no more crashes to find is more significant than it sounds. It’s common for fuzz tests in real-world code to test for violations of meaningful high-level properties, such as encode-decode roundtripping, idempotence, algebraic laws, differential testing, self-consistency, or equivalence to reference implementations. If the property does not hold, the program crashes—so proving the test never crashes is equivalent to proving the property itself.

This can also occur even when the properties are not directly specified by the developer. For example, in order for Claude to complete its OSS-Fuzz proof for cpp-httplib, it was necessary to rule out the possibility of a stack overflow due to too much recursion in the std::set destructor. #### Other formal verification case studies

Formal verification is an expansive domain. The fuzz-test-to-proof example above is one instance of LLMs making formal verification more widely usable by directly applying proofs to machine code.

We’ve also seen success using LLMs with formal verification in other ways. For example, we asked Claude to write a formal spec of RFC 1950, the technical document that defines the zlib compression file format. Then, we had Claude prove that the zlib implementation in the Linux kernel correctly implements that spec. We draw two conclusions from this exercise: (1) these extremely well-tested codebases are already almost fully correct, and (2) it is possible to prove end-to-end correctness properties about real existing codebases.

In another experiment, we asked Claude to develop an interpreter for a large subset of Python in Rust, and to prove (using Verus, a verification tool for Rust) that it adheres to the CPython semantics outlined in an academic paper. We also found issues in several widely used and critical applications via formal verification attempts of simple security properties. In one of them, we discovered a previously unknown logic bug that had been latent for more than a decade. ### This is just the beginning

One of the key limitations of LLM-assisted formal verification is that the proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens to produce. Cost-efficiency is critical if our goal is to make these methods available to the entire software ecosystem. Fortunately, there are compelling reasons to expect efficiency to improve.

#### Newer models need fewer tokens

We built 36 small verification tasks from real OSS-Fuzz code. Opus 5.5 proves half of them with about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. We expect this trend to continue as models are trained on long verification tasks.

#### Proofs can be reused

When agents work separately, they often end up duplicating a lot of effort. Proofs, like software, are recursively built from smaller proofs—and the smaller the proofs are, the more reusable they tend to be. To measure the impact of this, we let agents copy each other’s proofs as they worked on proving their own targets. When given access to this shared workspace, agents needed 17% fewer tokens than when they worked alone, and some agents even succeeded after previously failing in a solo attempt.

We observed the same phenomenon occurring at scale during our OSS-Fuzz proof effort. Most of a proof concerns code that every program contains (particularly initialization of the C runtime and AddressSanitizer), so very different programs can end up with significantly overlapping proofs. Agent teams took advantage of this by copying another team’s finished proof and then adapting it to their own program (Figure 6).

This reusability of proofs is how Mathlib, a shared library of formal mathematics in Lean, grew to nearly 300,000 theorems submitted by over 700 contributors: each new proof builds on the existing body of work. We accumulated a similar body of proofs in the course of our OSS-Fuzz effort, some of which we’re including in our release (we are not releasing proofs that may reveal an unpatched bug in the open-source software).

As we graduate from these initial experiments, we need a strategy for verifying the enormous body of existing software, starting with the most critical dependencies. As we’ve shown, this can be achieved at scale by using generic specs and working at the binary level, sidestepping the need to rewrite entire codebases in another language.

This approach also facilitates the reuse of proofs at package-level granularity, which means that each dependency only needs to be verified once. Dependencies follow a power law: proving even a small set of shared libraries makes a huge swath of software feasible to prove. For more details, see Theorem’s roadmap for verifying the entirety of the Nix ecosystem, which includes critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

### Limitations

In practice, formal verification can sometimes prove less about the security of the code than we would like.

“Formally verified” does not mean “bug-free.” Claude can write a proof showing that a compiled program’s behavior satisfies the requirements of a formal spec (which is verified by an external proof checker). However, a proof checker can’t tell you whether your spec matches reality. To match reality, the spec must correctly encompass and model everything about the real-world machine that the verified program runs on, including the CPU and operating system. When bugs show up in verified code, it’s because the spec, or the assumed semantics of the machine, differs from reality. Fortunately, this also means we know where to look for remaining bugs, and how to design a system where those still-possibly-buggy gaps are minimized. Below are the ways this applies to our proofs, and ideas for future work that would close those gaps.

The real machine does something the model doesn’t describe. Our proofs are about single-threaded, static RISC-V binaries linked against musl libc. However, most people run these libraries on x86 or ARM and dynamically link them against glibc. To close this gap, we’d need system models that more closely resemble deployed systems. For example, a step toward this would be generating accurate semantics for x86.

The claim may not cover everything we care about. We proved that a crash never triggers for any input under 64 MB on many fuzzing entry points in Google OSS-Fuzz, including ASan crashes. However, ASan doesn’t detect all memory safety bugs, and we didn’t verify all the entry points for each library. Even if we had, the whole library wouldn’t be covered by verifying all entry points (especially if there is dead code). Additionally, real programs might misuse the library, leading to memory corruption in the caller. To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.

### Conclusion

The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

### Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it. Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code.

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics. Theorem, our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects, and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

To close that gap, we’d need to specify what callers must do for each public function, and callers would have to strictly adhere to it.

We expect that as we learn more about leveraging LLMs for formal methods, and as models continue to improve, these limitations will become tractable, and we’ll be able to verify a much larger percentage of the code we rely upon.

### Conclusion

The trajectory is clear: formal verification, which was historically practical only for bespoke expert-crafted guarantees in the most safety-critical code, will soon be as practical as fuzzing is today for almost all production software. Just like static types, testing frameworks, and other correctness tooling, verification will mature from “bolted-on” to “built-in,” driven not only by LLMs but also by innovations in language design and development workflows.

In today’s world—where LLMs automatically scan for and find increasingly more code vulnerabilities—we must use processes that can guarantee code security properties. LLM-scaled formal verification is a promising approach toward securing these guarantees at a scope and scale that were previously unattainable. We encourage others to experiment so we can collectively build a world in which robust software has proliferated very widely and software bugs are a well-understood and quickly addressable rarity.

paragraphs: Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.
#### Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.
#### Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.
We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.
#### What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

subheadings: Methods for reducing codebases’ attack surface
paragraphs: Chris Rohlf

Over the past year, we’ve published lots of data that shows that frontier AI models are more than capable of discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities. Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense. In this post, we summarize some of our initial research into automated attack surface analysis and reduction: the process of using AI models to map the code that is reachable, then removing or restricting access to anything than a given deployment doesn’t need to expose.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. Securing software by finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities alone scales poorly: fixing even a critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the vulnerabilities that remain. By contrast, reducing code reachability can reduce the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including the ones that might be under active exploitation. These techniques don’t remove the unknown vulnerabilities in the code, but they do make the vulnerabilities harder to reach, and thereby reduce their severity. Minimizing codebases’ attack surface results in better security without ever having to find or fix an individual vulnerability.

Below, we preview some of the data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude. Our aim in doing so is to show that Claude can meaningfully, and economically, improve software security through the methods we outline. Specifically, we ran Claude over 25 projects (in a variety of languages), and it discovered 493 issues. With these results in mind, we discuss how developers can apply similar techniques to their own code.
#### Methods for reducing codebases’ attack surface

Over time, software has a tendency to become more complicated, with new layers of abstractions, new dependencies, and new features slowly piling on top of one-another. This can often cause it to function very differently to how its original developers intended. And it is a big part of why attackers are often so successful: they study exactly how a piece of code behaves in practice, rather than how its developers intended or designed it to work.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction techniques aim to discover unnecessary attack surfaces, then move that code behind an appropriate gate. This might involve moving code from pre-authentication to post-authentication, from 0-click to 1-click, from on-by-default to explicit opt-in, or from the first message of a protocol to deeper in the session state machine. Some code is meant to be reachable before these stages, but a lot it is not, and, given the complexity that comes with code churn across thousands or millions of lines of code, unnecessary exposure of features often goes unnoticed.
There are numerous ways to reduce the attack surface of code. In our own research efforts, we focused on three methods in particular:
• Default configuration. We identified code that was reachable in its shipped default configuration but wasn’t intended to be used by any default functionality.

• Configuration interaction. We found pairs of options that looked reasonable on their own, but which caused issues when configured together (for instance, by silently disabling a security control, or leaving a features behavior undefined while its code remains reachable).

• Early reachability. We identified security sensitive and complex code that runs either before an appropriate security control (such as authentication), without victim interaction, or before a protocol state transition.

We wanted to understand how well Claude could take these three descriptions of attack surface and discover real issues in large and complex codebases. We analyzed 25 open source projects (representing over five million lines of code), written in languages including C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python. Claude created an inventory of over 17,000 configuration options across these projects. Of those, 3,842 related to the configuration of a control or feature that was security relevant.
For the purposes of our research, we broke down these open source projects into three broad categories:

• Public. These projects are built to serve any user who can reach them, or to consume data authored by parties they cannot identify. (Examples include a DNS resolver parsing upstream answers, or a proxy parsing origin responses.)

• Gated. These projects are intended to serve authenticated users (such as those with a password, key or certificate holders, or enrolled devices). The software still allows for arbitrary client requests, but no functionality is available until the user has been authenticated.

• Private. These are built and deployed to serve the operator's own private environment. In these cases, adding a control like an authentication layer is optional, but outside the scope of the software.

These categories help to contextualize our results. For example, we’d expect a significant percentage of a Public codebase to be reachable in the default configuration (since it’s designed to serve any user), but the opposite to be true for projects in the Gated category.
#### Claude’s findings
Claude found 493 issues using the three methods described above. Several themes stuck out to us from its results.

First, Claude found that all eleven gated projects had code that was unintentionally reachable (although this code wasn’t a significant percentage of the total lines of code for any of those projects). Specifically, Claude discovered 93 unnecessary pre-authentication surfaces in the default configuration of the gated cohort, 37 locations where code executed, or state was recorded, before authentication, and 61 configuration combinations that silently weakened a pre-authentication control configured by the administrator. None of these issues would have been immediately exploitable on their own, but they create a much larger attack surface than is necessary.

Second, Claude’s work mitigating configuration interaction issues produced some of the most interesting and impactful findings (across all project types). Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction. In 94 of those cases, the combination silently turned off a security control. The other 68 cases were inconsistencies in the same security mechanisms (e.g. a listener or login path would remain reachable even though the configuration would say it was disabled; two settings would conflict, and the one that would take precedence would depend on their order in the configuration file, or a protection configured by the administrator would do nothing while its code remained reachable). While some of these configuration combinations might be non-standard or infrequently used, there would be nothing preventing an administrator of these projects from configuring and deploying the code in this way.

Claude also found one specific pattern that turned up independently in four unrelated projects. This would work as follows. An administrator would write an access rule for remote clients using a hostname or a wildcard pattern, instead of an IP address. When a client connects, the server would compare that rule against the client’s hostname. Whether the server ever learned that hostname would depend on a separate option that controlled reverse DNS lookups (which most projects had configured off). With lookups off, the server would only have the client’s IP address. The server would compare the rule against that address as plain text. But a hostname pattern can never match an IP address. This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open. Some of the affected projects mention in their documentation that hostname rules depend on DNS lookups being enabled, but none state that a deny list written this way would have fail open behavior.

Third, Claude often discovered that two configuration options would conflict in a way that silently dropped a security check. In one case, an administrator could require every connecting client to prove its identity with a certificate. In another, the code was only intended to delay that check until it was required, but in fact disabled the check entirely. A server that was configured to accept only trusted clients would therefore accept a connection from anyone. This exposed a large body of request handling code (which was supposed to be behind the certificate check) to unauthenticated clients. The software accepted both configuration options together with no warning under default settings; the documentation never mentioned that the certificate requirement had been dropped. This conflicting set of configuration options had been present in the software for 21 years.

Finally, Claude discovered an issue in a project that left authentication off by default (and expected the administrator to turn it on). The option that required TLS client certificates was honored on most of the project’s network endpoints, but silently ignored on a few others (ones which loaded their TLS settings through a path with a different namespace). This meant that a client with no certificate could complete the TLS handshake and open a session on an affected endpoint. Nothing would be logged about the ignored setting. Whether the option takes effect would depend on the namespace used by the administrator in the configuration. One form of the setting name works on every endpoint, but the shorter form—which most examples use—is dropped on the affected ones.
#### Case study: OpenSSH

Surprisingly, when measured as a percentage of the total lines of code, the project for which Claude achieved the largest reduction in attack surface was OpenSSH. OpenSSH is a high quality C codebase that provides secure remote access. Claude traced the input paths of the SSH daemon in the 10.4 release and found roughly 4,500 lines of new and experimental code for ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum signature algorithm, that an unauthenticated client could reach in the default configuration. ML-DSA is not enabled by default, but the code was reachable regardless, even when an administrator explicitly excluded the algorithm. The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed. There is no good reason for this complex, memory unsafe code to be reachable when it hasn’t been enabled by the configuration. Those 4,500 lines of code in ML-DSA-44 are about 16% of OpenSSH’s own pre-authentication code in a default sshd. We reported this to the OpenSSH developers along with patches. The 10.5 release moved the check before parsing.

Claude then noted two gaps in the 10.5 check. The first was a mismatch between what the client claimed and what it sent. The check looked at the algorithm name advertised by the client, but the parser was chosen by a type string embedded inside the key blob. A client could advertise ssh-ed25519, pass the check, and still send an ML-DSA key that would be parsed.

The second gap was in the 10.5 check’s certificates. Certificate key types were enabled by default. Given a certificate supplied by an attacker, sshd would deserialize the embedded CA public key and run a full signature verification with it, for any supported algorithm, before consulting the configuration. The user key signature path was properly gated behind the list of public keys allowed to connect to the server, but the CA signature path was not. That made every public key signature verifier in the binary reachable by any client that could complete a key exchange. We built a proof of concept and worked through several iterations of a fix with the maintainers. The resulting change placed the checks inside the parser itself. The encoded key type and the certificate’s CA signature algorithm are now compared against the configured allow lists before the corresponding deserialization or signature verification.

This fix removed roughly a fifth of the OpenSSH code that an unauthenticated client previously could have reached in a default build. Almost all of that was the new ML-DSA code, which is now unreachable even for a client that lies about its key type or hides an ML-DSA CA key inside an otherwise acceptable certificate. Certificates signed with an allowed CA algorithm are still parsed and verified, but the check now runs before parsing. The maintainers shipped the changes described here in version 10.6.

OpenSSH is some of the most heavily audited code in the world. If unnecessary reachability survives there, it can survive anywhere. This suggests that reducing the attack surface of codebases is likely to pay dividends across many important codebases.
#### Conclusion

It is perhaps impossible to measure how many unknown vulnerabilities are in any given codebase. And there is plenty of data that shows attackers can and will find those vulnerabilities with enough time (particularly if equipped with frontier AI models). But a defender who reduces unnecessary attack surface in their code reduces the risk from all of the unknown vulnerabilities in that code at once—including any that are already being quietly exploited. OpenSSH is some of the most audited C code in the world. Yet it shipped around 4,500 lines of experimental signature parsing code that could have been reached by an attacker prior to any configuration check.

We have combined the attack surface reduction techniques we described above into one reusable Claude skill, which we are working to integrate into OSS-Scanner. The skill runs three passes on a codebase. Each time it starts fresh (with an empty context window), except for a short piece of context it receives from the prior pass.

In the first pass, the skill looks at whether there is code that the default configuration allows to be reached but which isn’t used by any intended functionality. In the second pass, it looks at the code that runs before any hard gates (like authentication) or before protocol state machine entry points, in any configuration. Finally, third, the skill assesses which combinations of configurations silently switch a security control off or degrade its efficacy. In every pass, Claude creates an inventory of the entry points from the code and confirms each finding with a dynamic trace of the program. For default configuration findings, it designs and implements a gate and ensures that this causes no change in the program’s default behavior. It does so by running the project's own test suite (along with a black box regression suite) against the baseline; it requires modified builds to have identical results. Any gate that would change a non-default configuration is set aside for a human to decide. For the other two passes, it proposes changes like reordering a configuration check, adding a guard to enforce state ordering, or rejecting the combination at configuration load. Even without using this specific skill, we think the broad methodology outlined here is likely to be effective.

The techniques outlined in this post offer only a very limited view into what is possible in attack surface reduction. For instance, Claude is also capable of analyzing and comparing runtime logs against configurations to ensure that only required functionality has been enabled: disabling unused parsers, legacy protocols, and dashboards reduces security risk at little cost.

We encourage organizations to explore using Claude to analyze and reduce the attack surface of the software they depend on. We expect this to be one of the most practical ways that developers can measurably improve the security of the code the world already runs on.

Over time, software has a tendency to become more complicated, with new layers of abstractions, new dependencies, and new features slowly piling on top of one-another.
