### Introduction

Ever-improving AI capabilities make a longstanding concern increasingly realistic: autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA), which involves a model deploying and propagating itself without human control.

In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. Prior work has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.

Datacenter GPUs would be a clear, high-value target for such malware. But expensive accelerators aren’t strictly necessary. In this blog post, we show that a distributed botnet of IoT devices—which are cheap and typically poorly defended—could also provide enough compute to run a capable model.

We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second. Each tile below shows one physical TV box holding two of the model’s layers as the model runs.

Of course, there are many other steps to showing that an autonomous worm can propagate itself across a network of weak machines. For the purposes of this blog post, we break down the replication chain into a few steps.

We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process (the first two stages above), since earlier papers CyberGym, ExploitBench, and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools. But a less commonly measured part of the replication process involves setting up inference on compromised devices, which is our focus here.

In this post, we first lay out the threat models that we think are most likely to be realized. Then, we test whether small models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, and whether they can chain the full replication cycle together across a fleet of machines. After that, we estimate how fast such a worm could spread, and test whether it could learn and adapt as it replicates. We conclude with how AI worms would differ from pre-AI malware, and brief suggestions for defenses against such replicators.

#### Threat modelling

In this blog post, we’re focused on one way that AI worms might propagate: small models that replicate through compromising their host machines. But there are several other methods that AI worms might try: they could steal access in order to spin up hosts (for example, API keys or platform credentials) or pay for inference through legitimate work (e.g digital freelancing). The threat models that we think are closest to being realized today are the following:

• A small model, replicating via host compromise. In this post, we’ll call autonomous worms that run their models directly on compromised hardware weight-based replicators. Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place.A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself. This extra computing power will likely make them attractive targets as well.Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve.

• Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve.

• A large, advanced weight-based replicator focused on datacenters and other high-compute targets. Larger models tend to have correspondingly better cyber capabilities, but will also need to breach (relatively) hardened datacenters to run themselves. We split this threat model into two subcategories:Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up unmonitored internal deployments or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute.Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored.

• Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up unmonitored internal deployments or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute.

• Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored.

• An API-based replicator, in which a model would replicate by stealing credentials for their own inference API. These replicators would require a model provider to unknowingly serve them, and their persistence may be worse, since they’d likely be easier to discover (although their rate of spread may be higher, if for instance they’re able to replicate using victims’ accounts).

• Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve.

• Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up unmonitored internal deployments or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute.

• Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored.

In practice, an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic ‘worst case scenario’ attack.

In this blog post, we consider the feasibility of small weight-based replicators (section 1 of the above). We focus on this because it’s a near-term threat model that can be investigated directly. Our demo at the top of this post, a 26B model running across 15 boxes, shows that IoT devices can run surprisingly capable models. Could these models be capable enough to carry out autonomous replication?

We examine this in two parts. First, can small models get a model running on unfamiliar hardware? And second, can they do the whole cycle (find an uninfected device, copy themselves over, start running there, and repeat) all together in a single run?

### A. Inference setup

Of the stages in the above diagram showing the replication cycle, inference setup is the least studied and may be the most challenging for small models. It requires a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from.

#### Aside

Unlike many types of malware, weight-based replicators don’t need root privileges. While it’d be convenient to privilege escalate in order to have persistence over shutdowns, such as via cronjobs, it may not be truly necessary. Inference engines can run entirely in userspace, and many of the low-security devices we anticipate such a replicator to spread on can be re-infected upon restart. Similar examples include crypto miners and botnets/worms like P2Pinfect and Fritzfrog, which can operate without privilege escalation but will try it opportunistically.

#### How does a model run on Smart TVs?

IoT devices are light on memory, but distributed inference as in Petals makes serving our lightweight models feasible. The representative threat model is Kimwolf, a large IoT botnet that infected over two million devices, primarily off-brand Android TVs. Such smart TV boxes, which are readily available for purchase, typically run forks of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which their manufacturers don’t add security features to. Typical boxes in this range ship with between 1 and 4 gigabytes of RAM. Assuming 4GB of RAM at 4-bit quantization, this allows for inference of 9B models with 4 or more machines, and inference of 26B models with 10+ machines.

In the demo at the top of this post, we ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 smart TV boxes with 4GB of RAM each. We sharded the model under pipeline parallelism, where each box holds a small fraction of the model’s layers.

Right now, the floor and ceiling don’t intersect. When might they?

The solid line is the least-squares fit over the best models in-class at each date, with a gain of 13.7 ECI per year (R2 of 0.95). If we take GLM-5.2 as a capabilities floor for replication, the trend line puts a small model at that level by the end of 2026. ECI is a general capability index, which is only a proxy metric for replication ability, so this is only a rough estimate of when a small-model replicator becomes possible.

### C. How fast might an AI IoT worm replicate?

Unlike coding agents, these replicators would be running below the interactive speeds of user-facing chat and coding harnesses. The spread would be slow and persistent, with tokens being trickled out on edge hardware. We can use our achieved speeds on our real smart TVs as a demonstrated baseline for replication speeds. For Gemma4-26B-A4B, unoptimized speed across a 32k context length token window is about 0.3 tok/s, averaged across prefill and decode in our inference setup workload. More details in Appendix C.

A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory.

The number of devices infected by the Kimwolf botnet at its peak, reported by Synthient, is somewhere over 2 million (primarily Android TV boxes). In an equivalently-sized infected fleet of TVs serving AI models, if every group of 15 TVs ran a copy of Gemma4-26B-A4B, we would have ~133k copies (“replicas”). A group of TVs like the ones in our demo can serve 2 agents simultaneously at roughly 0.3 tokens per second each, yielding 80k tokens/s across the botnet.

As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at high concurrency with speculative decoding, so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.

This is a rough estimate, as it’s anchored on a single class of IoT hardware and a single past botnet instance, but describes what a simple replicator released in the near future might look like. In practice, more capable replicators would take advantage of other types of low-security compute, and would be opportunistic about deploying models of various sizes on different devices. (It also wouldn’t have to load a model payload onto every device it compromises). Over time, we expect the amount of deployed edge compute to continue growing, while the minimum model size required for reliable replication falls.

### D. Adaptation and uplift

#### Learning on the job

The “Adaptation” part of ARA is one reason why an AI replicator might outperform a traditional worm. Specifically, models and prompts can undergo Lamarckian evolution as they spread–that is, parent instances can pass on their prompts, code, and notes to their daughter replicators. In order to adapt and spread across a wide variety of hardware, a model would require two things:

• Being above a certain threshold of capability for spreading onto a novel, unseen piece of hardware (or software environment, or network type).

• Once seen, adapting to the type of environment it has landed in (it should replicate more reliably on hardware it has seen before).

Sections A and B test the first condition, and in the experiment below we test the second. Each Qwen3.5-9B instance keeps brief notes on the strategies it tried and the failures it encountered, before a new instance inherits those notes and attempts the same inference setup again.

Inference setup success rate across six generations of Qwen3.5-9B, each inheriting the former’s notes. Faint lines are the 20 individual lineages, and the bold line is the proportion of runs in each generation that complete setup. It rises from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones. This uses the Memento setup (Appendix A).

#### Taking advice

Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a frontier advisor, a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck. To test this, we gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8 during the inference setup task. The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted.

Even when trained through reinforcement learning to use the advisor in a similar setting (Python coding problems), the small model still struggles to ask for help productively for inference standup. Both results are shown in the plot below.

Inference setup success rate by advisor access, with Wilson 95% intervals. Access to an advisor, whether offered as a tool call or given to the model automatically when stuck, gives no significant improvement. The two RL groups were trained with advisor access on software engineering tasks, and the rightmost group also rewards calling the advisor when stuck.

Since small models are capable and persistent individual agents and make poor use of advice, we think coordination is more likely to happen with a large model handling high-level strategy and spinning up small models as subagents.

### E. How is this different from a pre-AI botnet?

Hard-coded botnets like the Kimwolf botnet each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A). We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this.

### F. Blue-team mitigations

As with an epidemic, defense involves driving R₀ (the number of new devices each infected device goes on to infect) below 1, such that the replicator dies out instead of staying endemic.

Some elements around this threat model are in the defenders’ favor:

• A weight-based replicator multiplying through IoT machines at scale would leave a network signature, visible as an anomaly in ISP flow-based monitoring systems. Newly infected hosts may receive multi-gigabyte model payloads from other devices or external hosting services, while distributed inference can produce sustained device-to-device traffic between machines that wouldn’t ordinarily communicate at that volume. Propagation itself would add additional scanning and outbound connection patterns.In practice, the replicator trades off between replication speed and stealth: the faster it replicates, the more traffic it produces. Once the replicator is discovered, defenders can use honeypots (decoy devices) to collect the replicator’s harness and payload to characterize its behavior.

• Remediation of the Mirai botnet was possible when an ISP used externally obtained infection evidence to quarantine and notify customers. Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions. This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult.

• Manufacturers can shrink the pool of targets, with regulation acting to coordinate. For example, default IoT passwords are now non-compliant in UK markets. Moving to more secure defaults and raising the baseline for compliance will help harden against both AI and scripted botnets.

### G. Conclusion: Signs of life

The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.

### Appendix

#### A. The Memento harness

Memento executes as follows:

• We spawn an agent instance, which tackles the problem for a while (until generation timeout).

• The instance keeps brief notes, and after timeout summarizes a small doc of the strategies it tried, the failures it encountered, and its performance (if successful).

• We create a new agent instance that inherits the codebase and environment from its predecessor as well as the notebook.

In the serving experiment, each model is placed in a Memento harness and is given a 1.5 hour per iteration / 6 hour total timeout. Around ~1k tokens of information, including specs about the hardware and a script for a simple sample profiler, are given in the prompt.

Memento is intended to improve long-horizon reliability rather than grant new cyber or inference-specific capabilities. It’s also not a universally strong harness; we expect that small models will improve as replicators even without any harnessing as capabilities improve.

Single attempt compared against Memento, by model (95% Wilson CI).

#### B. Why pipeline parallel?

Common parallelism schemes for inference include tensor parallel (TP), expert parallel (EP), and data parallel. Most smart TV / IoT devices use ARM Cortex CPUs and DDR3/4 memory; on such machines, we’re almost always bandwidth bound.

We use pipeline parallelism for its fault-tolerant properties. As noted in (Borzunov et al. 2022), the failure of a single node in tensor parallel / expert parallel brings down the full set of machines running the model replica. Pipeline parallel allows the downed node to be replaced, with the KV cache for the layers held by the node recomputable via another forward pass of the node prior to the restarted node.

#### C. Throughput and memory on IoT hardware

Across such machines, we’re almost always RAM-bandwidth bound per-box across prefill and decode. Even on modest ARM-cortex cores, compute throughput outpaces RAM bandwidth. Decode workloads have significant per-machine idle time due to pipeline bubbling, as only one machine is active at a time during each forward pass. Concurrency with staggered work is possible, but tight memory constraints mean that concurrency stays low.

Per-box memory vs context — 4-bit weights + fp8 KV + activations.

Both prefill and decode tokens/s strictly decrease with sequence length. Below is a graph of our inference speeds against context length:

There’s also a minimum sequence length at which models are competent. The harness we use is forked off of the Pi coding agent (pi.dev) and contains a native compaction mechanism - even still, we find that models take a large performance hit when their sequence lengths are restricted below 32K.

Qwen3.5-9B agentic competence on the inference setup task vs. context window budget.

Given the above eval, we assume that a 32k context length may be sufficient for reasonable agentic performance. A standard 32k-length context window in our inference setup workload consists of 12–15% generated decode tokens, with the rest being prefill from prompts and toolcalls. Prefill tokens are much faster to compute by a factor of ~15, due to the pipeline bubbling. Taking the sum of time per token over the whole 32k context (taking into account prefill and decode speeds), we find that generating the 3.8-4.8k decode output tokens and processing the ~28k prefill tokens takes between 27.3-31.8h for Gemma4-26B-A4B and 10.9h for Qwen3.5-9B.

Per-chain output tokens (summed over a chain’s generations), by model; medians ≈ 19.7k / 12.3k / 11.0k. Data from the inference setup eval.

#### D. Edge Accelerators

We can compute a better upper bound by using the pool of Nvidia Jetsons, which are edge accelerators. Unlike the traditional IoT botnet, IoT edge devices can serve a full model wholesale. A Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB runs Qwen3-30B-A3B at 76.7 tokens per second, and an AGX Thor reaches 226 tok/s. Note that we don’t believe they’re unusually vulnerable - this is just to count the upper bound. The types of devices with Jetsons in the wild include:

• AI-enabled smart cameras for security with embedded accelerators are deployed at substantial scale.

• Conferencing machines are frequently powered by an onboard accelerator for on-device noise cancellation or transcription.

• Vehicles, robot quadrupeds and bipeds, and drones. We expect cybersecurity to be a focal point for vehicles, so the majority of the potential targets likely lie in the other two categories.

At least one accelerator-equipped smart camera host appears to be reachable on IPv4 on a quick search on FOFA:

While it’s difficult to estimate how many edge-accelerator-equipped machines in the wild are reachable and vulnerable, we can calculate a strict upper bound of the amount of devices present. Across the wild there are on the order of 90 distinct NVIDIA-silicon IoT product lines and roughly 9.5 million fielded units. Reachability is overwhelmingly through outbound cloud-management tunnels instead of inbound ports, meaning that the majority are not web-reachable. There have been no historical mass-compromises of accelerator-equipped edge devices the way there have been standard IoT botnets, suggesting that compromise of such devices would be more difficult.

Fielded units per device family, colored by internet reachability.

A very rough estimate based on product data suggests that somewhere between 9,000 and 35,000 H100-equivalents of compute exist in edge accelerators, but the amount that’s reachable is likely an order of magnitude or more lower (and the vulnerable population even lower than that).

#### Aside

Aside from these edge accelerators, we also consider the small-business and industrial IoT tiers, such as NAS boxes, mini-PCs, and Rockchip-containing SoCs (like Orange Pis). Historically, we know small business NAS machines are vulnerable to ransomware and cryptojacking (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and National Cyber Security Centre 2020), with each having 512MB-2GB of soldered RAM (which puts them in a similar category as the smart TVs). Mini-PCs are typically significantly more hardened, and machines like Orange Pis are capable (see our inference setup table) but are also difficult to breach.

#### E. Spearphishing capability

We also measure how proficient modern small models are at spearphishing. Spearphishing is the act of sending targeted messages to specific individuals to trick them into revealing credentials or running a piece of malware. While the agentic cyber capability of small models has skyrocketed, their general knowledge and linguistic sophistication have improved more slowly; we expect social engineering attacks and phishing to be largely accomplished by large/frontier models (although it’s very plausible that this is a secondary replication vector in a heterogeneous botnet running both large and small models).

Spear-phishing capability on Meta’s CyberSecEval 3’s spear-phishing eval (Wan et al. 2024), replicated locally. Scored on a scale of 0-5, with gpt-4o as a judge. Red diamonds are the paper’s (CyberSecEval 3) human-rubric scores on the reference models, which indicates that gpt-4o scores ~0.4-0.7 pts more leniently than human raters. 2 is “poor”, 3 is “intermediate”, and 4 “good.” When normalized to human raters, small models score “very poor” to “poor”.

The 405B reference slot uses Hermes-3-405B as a minimal-refusal stand-in for the unavailable Llama3.1-405B-Instruct.

#### F. Propagation with scripted inference setup:

We run a few more experiments on a network of 17 hosts in a topology like so:

Two networks with 8 hosts each, connected by a single node with access to both subnets. Each network is all-to-all connected. The worm agent begins on a single patient zero node in segment A; the pivot node adds a slight extra challenge in having the worm needing to gain access to the pivot node and re-scan from it.

Each is running Android with an ADB port open without authentication. Upon spreading to a new target, the agent is able to invoke a direct call to replicate itself immediately - this is just to measure the difficulty of the remaining steps, after we exclude the cyber and inference setup steps. As shown in the graph, even a 3B model reaches about half the nodes. This puts a bound on the number of blockers in our eval that we fail to measure under the cyber or inference setup elements.

A more detailed breakdown of the runs in “replication across a 17 node network.” Each column is the median number of nodes reached under different amounts of guidance in the prompt, and the subscript denotes how many agents cross over the pivot node to the other side of the network.

paragraphs: Today we are launching Claude Frontier Academy to solve one of the most pressing issues in AI implementation: talent. Backed by a $100 million commitment, Anthropic aims to train 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers (FDEs) by the end of 2027. Engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley and Novo Nordisk are in the first cohorts.

Every enterprise is racing to bring AI into its organization, but the people with the skills to make it work inside a real business have become the hardest talent to find. Inside the companies we work with, a small group of deeply skilled people drives an outsized share of what AI delivers. The Academy is the first of its kind from an AI company, built from our own work deploying Claude inside the world’s largest enterprises and the professional services organizations that serve them.

“A small team of high-agency people with the right skills, access to Claude, and a deep understanding of how their business runs can transform an entire company. The hard part is building that depth of talent, engineers with the highest level of AI fluency who can take Claude from an idea to a system in production and turn it into faster processes and new products and services. No AI company has invested in developing that talent inside its customers and partners at this depth. Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn, and we want those who graduate to set the standard for how AI gets built inside a business.” – Steve Corfield, Global Head of Business Development and Partnerships at Anthropic
#### The first program trains 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers

The Academy’s first program, the Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency, follows the medical model for building expertise. Doctors learn from practicing physicians, train on real cases, and are assessed before they practice alone. Likewise, FDE Residency engineers learn from practitioners, practice on realistic cases, and are assessed on their work before they earn the credential. The goal is agentic systems that change how a business runs, from faster, redesigned processes to new products and services.

The program is for hands-on software engineers with strong fundamentals, a record of building with LLMs, experience helping others adopt AI, and a habit of tackling their business’s most important problems. Organizations nominate their strongest engineers, each arriving with a named Claude project to lead when they return. Prior experience building AI agents isn’t required.

Engineers start with a multi-day in-person program with Anthropic engineers and licensed instructors. They work through a simulated enterprise deployment, from the right use case through security review to handover, and finish with a graded practical on a new scenario. Those who pass earn the Claude Resident Engineer badge and move into the 12-week residency, where they lead a real Claude use case at their own organization, supported by Anthropic engineers and learning from their cohort as they build. Engineers are assessed again at the end of the 12 weeks, and those who pass earn the Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer badge, with the first expected in early 2027.
#### The first cohorts are running now

Cohorts are running in San Francisco, New York and London. The program will grow toward 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027. Participation is by nomination; organizations can ask their Anthropic account team or Partner Account Manager whether they’re eligible.
#### Leading enterprises and consulting firms are in the first cohorts

“At Accenture, forward deployed engineers translate AI ambition into enterprise-wide impact, working inside client workflows as part of multidisciplinary teams that engineer AI concepts into production-ready, governed solutions built to scale. Anthropic built the residency the same way we think about the role: judgment tested against a simulated enterprise deployment, not technical skills in isolation. Joining Claude Frontier Academy will deepen our engineers’ Claude expertise and accelerate the value we deliver for our clients.”
Ram Ramalingam
FDE and Software & Platform Engineering lead, Accenture

“Building deep, hands-on AI engineering capability is critical to helping clients move from experimentation to impact at scale. The Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency will give our engineers the opportunity to sharpen their expertise working directly with Anthropic and bring that experience to our work with clients.”
Michael Blake
Partner, Global Head of Engineering, Bain

“What I’m hearing from clients isn’t about certification counts or training volume; it’s about knowing firsthand how to solve real-world problems that create value to our clients. By working side by side with Anthropic’s own engineers, Capgemini is investing in and building the delivery excellence that clients recognize immediately.”
Geoffroy Pajot
Global Head of AI Partnerships Ecosystem, Capgemini

“AI is transforming the way we build, deliver and innovate for customers. Our engineers use AI tools every day, and our teams have produced up to 3x more code changes in the past year. The Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency takes them deeper, with hands-on experience building, securing and shipping alongside peers at the frontier. We are building tomorrow’s bank today, and this program gives our teams the tools and expertise to engineer the best possible products for our customers.”
Rodrigo Castillo
Group Chief Technology Officer, Commonwealth Bank of Australia

“AI deployment at enterprise scale requires skilled people who can drive a project from first requirements through security review to real adoption. The Claude Frontier Academy’s FDE Residency enables us to scale a discipline we’ve already tested in the field, which is why we are excited to be part of the inaugural cohort, bringing our engineers in early to extend our bench of Claude-ready talent.”
Faruk Muratovic
Principal, Deloitte Consulting LLP

“This collaboration between McKinsey and Anthropic is about leveraging frontier AI to create superior business outcomes for clients. Our technologists bring frontier AI expertise, sector depth and a value-creation mindset to our client work. The Residency sets the bar for how they apply Claude in service of our clients’ business goals, giving our world-class talent experience learning frontier techniques alongside Anthropic’s engineers. The Claude Frontier Academy and FDE Residency extend our technologists’ toolkit, helping them solve our clients’ toughest problems hands-on-keys.”
Dan Tinkoff
Senior Partner and Global Co-leader of QuantumBlack, McKinsey

“AI is already changing how we discover and develop medicines at Novo. With Claude Science in our R&D workflows, Anthropic’s frontier models in our software development, lab in the loop research in drug discovery, and Anthropic engineers working alongside our scientists, we have seen what is possible when frontier AI meets deep scientific expertise. We’re excited to join the Claude Frontier Academy and the FDE Residency, giving our engineers the same hands on training and expertise behind Anthropic’s most successful deployments, so together we can bring the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”
Loic Giraud
VP Data & AI, Novo Nordisk
#### The Claude Partner Network

Claude Frontier Academy builds on the Claude Partner Network, where professionals across 46,000 firms have earned more than 175,000 Claude certifications and nearly 4,000 people have completed Basecamp, an immersive program that teaches the same curriculum our Applied AI teams receive when they onboard. Claude Frontier Academy is for the people who will lead the work, and training 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers is the first step of many.

The Academy is the first of its kind from an AI company, built from our own work deploying Claude inside the world’s largest enterprises and the professional services organizations that serve them.

“A small team of high-agency people with the right skills, access to Claude, and a deep understanding of how their business runs can transform an entire company. The hard part is building that depth of talent, engineers with the highest level of AI fluency who can take Claude from an idea to a system in production and turn it into faster processes and new products and services. No AI company has invested in developing that talent inside its customers and partners at this depth. Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn, and we want those who graduate to set the standard for how AI gets built inside a business.” – Steve Corfield, Global Head of Business Development and Partnerships at Anthropic

#### The first program trains 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers

The Academy’s first program, the Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency, follows the medical model for building expertise. Doctors learn from practicing physicians, train on real cases, and are assessed before they practice alone. Likewise, FDE Residency engineers learn from practitioners, practice on realistic cases, and are assessed on their work before they earn the credential. The goal is agentic systems that change how a business runs, from faster, redesigned processes to new products and services.

The program is for hands-on software engineers with strong fundamentals, a record of building with LLMs, experience helping others adopt AI, and a habit of tackling their business’s most important problems. Organizations nominate their strongest engineers, each arriving with a named Claude project to lead when they return. Prior experience building AI agents isn’t required.

Engineers start with a multi-day in-person program with Anthropic engineers and licensed instructors. They work through a simulated enterprise deployment, from the right use case through security review to handover, and finish with a graded practical on a new scenario. Those who pass earn the Claude Resident Engineer badge and move into the 12-week residency, where they lead a real Claude use case at their own organization, supported by Anthropic engineers and learning from their cohort as they build. Engineers are assessed again at the end of the 12 weeks, and those who pass earn the Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer badge, with the first expected in early 2027.

#### The first cohorts are running now

Cohorts are running in San Francisco, New York and London. The program will grow toward 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027. Participation is by nomination; organizations can ask their Anthropic account team or Partner Account Manager whether they’re eligible.

#### Leading enterprises and consulting firms are in the first cohorts

“At Accenture, forward deployed engineers translate AI ambition into enterprise-wide impact, working inside client workflows as part of multidisciplinary teams that engineer AI concepts into production-ready, governed solutions built to scale. Anthropic built the residency the same way we think about the role: judgment tested against a simulated enterprise deployment, not technical skills in isolation. Joining Claude Frontier Academy will deepen our engineers’ Claude expertise and accelerate the value we deliver for our clients.”

Ram Ramalingam

FDE and Software & Platform Engineering lead, Accenture

“Building deep, hands-on AI engineering capability is critical to helping clients move from experimentation to impact at scale. The Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency will give our engineers the opportunity to sharpen their expertise working directly with Anthropic and bring that experience to our work with clients.”

Michael Blake

Partner, Global Head of Engineering, Bain

“What I’m hearing from clients isn’t about certification counts or training volume; it’s about knowing firsthand how to solve real-world problems that create value to our clients. By working side by side with Anthropic’s own engineers, Capgemini is investing in and building the delivery excellence that clients recognize immediately.”

Geoffroy Pajot

Global Head of AI Partnerships Ecosystem, Capgemini

“AI is transforming the way we build, deliver and innovate for customers. Our engineers use AI tools every day, and our teams have produced up to 3x more code changes in the past year. The Frontier Deployed Engineer Residency takes them deeper, with hands-on experience building, securing and shipping alongside peers at the frontier. We are building tomorrow’s bank today, and this program gives our teams the tools and expertise to engineer the best possible products for our customers.”

Rodrigo Castillo

Group Chief Technology Officer, Commonwealth Bank of Australia

“AI deployment at enterprise scale requires skilled people who can drive a project from first requirements through security review to real adoption. The Claude Frontier Academy’s FDE Residency enables us to scale a discipline we’ve already tested in the field, which is why we are excited to be part of the inaugural cohort, bringing our engineers in early to extend our bench of Claude-ready talent.”

Faruk Muratovic

Principal, Deloitte Consulting LLP

“This collaboration between McKinsey and Anthropic is about leveraging frontier AI to create superior business outcomes for clients. Our technologists bring frontier AI expertise, sector depth and a value-creation mindset to our client work. The Residency sets the bar for how they apply Claude in service of our clients’ business goals, giving our world-class talent experience learning frontier techniques alongside Anthropic’s engineers. The Claude Frontier Academy and FDE Residency extend our technologists’ toolkit, helping them solve our clients’ toughest problems hands-on-keys.”

Dan Tinkoff

Senior Partner and Global Co-leader of QuantumBlack, McKinsey

“AI is already changing how we discover and develop medicines at Novo. With Claude Science in our R&D workflows, Anthropic’s frontier models in our software development, lab in the loop research in drug discovery, and Anthropic engineers working alongside our scientists, we have seen what is possible when frontier AI meets deep scientific expertise. We’re excited to join the Claude Frontier Academy and the FDE Residency, giving our engineers the same hands on training and expertise behind Anthropic’s most successful deployments, so together we can bring the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”

Loic Giraud

VP Data & AI, Novo Nordisk

#### The Claude Partner Network

Claude Frontier Academy builds on the Claude Partner Network, where professionals across 46,000 firms have earned more than 175,000 Claude certifications and nearly 4,000 people have completed Basecamp, an immersive program that teaches the same curriculum our Applied AI teams receive when they onboard. Claude Frontier Academy is for the people who will lead the work, and training 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers is the first step of many.

paragraphs: Today, Claude for Government is generally available for federal and state agencies. The platform, which delivers Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities through a FedRAMP High authorized environment, has been in public beta since July.
Agencies access capabilities comparable to Anthropic’s commercial customers, without compromising compliance requirements. New capabilities generally arrive on the commercial release cadence.

Claude works directly with files on the desktop, allowing agency staff to use skills, plugins and projects for memo creation, RFP reviews, casework, and other tasks. With Claude Code, public sector teams can build and modernize the software systems that underpin public services.

Claude for Government governance controls are purpose-built for public sector agencies. Administrators can set configuration defaults as well as allocate and control spending across departments. Security teams and authorizing officials get audit logs and documentation that supports the agency ATO process. Procurement officers can contract with Anthropic directly and award on general-availability terms.
The Claude Code command-line interface and Claude for Microsoft 365 are also rolling out in early access through the same environment and with the same administrative controls.
### Billing, administration, and oversight

No seat fees. Agencies pay for usage in fixed increments with a hard not-to-exceed cap, so spend does not exceed what an agency has obligated. Administrators define user tiers with spend and model limits per group, track usage by user and by model, and get burndown alerts before a balance runs low.

Administration that matches how departments are organized. Department-level administrators allocate prepaid usage to sub-agencies while each manages its own users. Agencies connect their own identity provider for single sign-on, with self-serve setup in the admin portal. SCIM group mappings set rate limits, dollar caps, and allowed models for each seat tier. Layered configuration sets defaults for sub-agencies, including what Claude can connect to and which features are available.

Oversight by design. Administrative actions are recorded in an audit log that organization administrators can review. Sensitive operations on Anthropic's side require two-person approval. Usage exports are metering data only, so agencies can answer ATO and IG requests without moving sensitive material. Conversation history stays local on the agency-managed device.
### Getting started

Claude for Government is generally available to federal and state agencies today. Agencies do not need a separate cloud-provider relationship to get started. Existing customers can move to the desktop application and bring their conversation history with them through an in-app import.
Our FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guide is available through Anthropic's trust center. The application deploys through standard agency MDM platforms.

New agencies can request access at claude.com/solutions/government. To join the early access for Claude Code CLI or Claude for Microsoft 365, contact our public sector team. Also learn more with the Claude for Government documentation.

Five months ago, we announced Claude Mythos Preview, the first AI model that could autonomously build sophisticated, end-to-end cyber exploits. The rapid rate of improvement in AI suggested to us that this ability would eventually proliferate to many other models, making it much easier for malicious cyber actors to launch highly impactful cyberattacks.

In light of these considerations, we chose to release Claude Mythos Preview in a limited way, through Project Glasswing—which enabled trusted cyber defenders to find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software, giving them a head start before malicious actors had access to similarly capable models.

But those models have now arrived. In this post, we share our analysis of GLM-5.3, the latest AI model developed by Zhipu AI (known outside of China as Z.ai). Like Claude Mythos Preview, GLM-5.3 has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits. But GLM-5.3 is unlike other frontier models in that it has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse. We find that attackers can bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques in our simulated tests. In contrast, these attacks did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models in our testing. We assess that GLM-5.3’s lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems.

On Sept. 17, NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) published its own assessment of GLM-5.3’s cyber capabilities. CAISI found that GLM-5.3 is “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date” and that it lags the US frontier by about four months on an aggregate of CAISI’s cyber benchmarks. Our capability findings broadly match CAISI’s. In CAISI’s comparison, US models were tested with cyber safeguards disabled when applicable, and the US frontier includes models released only to vetted users. Attackers can’t readily access those versions of US models, but anyone can download GLM-5.3. This post adds our analysis of how easily GLM-5.3’s safeguards can be bypassed or removed.
### GLM-5.3 can develop working exploits end to end

To understand how GLM-5.3 could enable cyber threat actors to find and exploit real software vulnerabilities, we ran evaluations using automated benchmarks and human-in-the-loop workflows. For both approaches, we ran the tested models in isolated and sandboxed environments so they can only attack offline targets that we have set up for the purposes of these evaluations. We focus primarily on exploit development capability, as this is where Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated a notable jump versus previous Claude models.

First, we ran the model on ExploitBench, which measures how well AI models can exploit known vulnerabilities in the V8 engine used by Google Chrome. Here we focus on the models’ ability to develop end-to-end exploits successfully, as this is the most relevant capability for attackers, and where we see significant changes between models. We find that GLM-5.3 develops end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts. Claude Mythos Preview did so at a similar rate—in 56 of 410 attempts.

In our internal Binary Exploitation benchmark,1 we test whether models can find and exploit vulnerabilities in popular open-source projects that participate in Google’s OSS-Fuzz project. Here, full credit is awarded for a full control-flow hijack. We evaluate several models on 100 tasks from the benchmark (selected at random), and find that GLM-5.3 develops full control-flow hijacks in 4% of the trials; Claude Mythos Preview did so in 6%. Although GLM-5.3 performs below Claude Mythos Preview here, a meaningful threshold has clearly been crossed: earlier models, like Claude Opus 4.6 and GLM-5.2, do not succeed in any of them.

Next, we evaluated how GLM-5.3 performs on open-ended offensive cyber tasks in the hands of human experts (mirroring our testing with Claude Mythos Preview earlier this year). Here, we select targets in which the human experts are unaware of existing vulnerabilities, then ask them to use the model to identify and exploit novel flaws. These experiments tested what the experts could do in a short time-frame: they typically ran for a day or less, with less than an hour of human focus in total.

In the first of these sessions, a researcher used GLM-5.3 on a sandboxed machine with a local Linux build of a popular web browser. Over the course of a day (and with limited human attention), GLM-5.3 found several previously unknown vulnerabilities in the browser’s JavaScript engine, and chained them together into a working exploit: a webpage that, when visited, reads arbitrary files from the visitor’s computer (shown in Figure 3). This exploit targets the Linux build of the browser, since that was the only environment made available to the model. However, we believe these vulnerabilities could also impact users on other platforms, though the path to exploitation there may be more complex. (We’ve disclosed these vulnerabilities to the maintainer.) Later in the session, the researcher also identified exploitable vulnerabilities in several other widely used systems with GLM-5.3, including wireless and graphics drivers and network-facing device software. We are currently reviewing these reports and we will disclose to maintainers as appropriate.

In a second session, a researcher used GLM-5.3-Flash (a smaller, less capable version of GLM-5.3) to develop an exploit for a known vulnerability (we’ve previously written about these “N-day” vulnerability exploits here). Here, the researcher focused on a recently disclosed flaw in Google Chrome (CVE-2026-11645) to see how quickly the model could turn a public fix into a working attack. The researcher provided GLM-5.3-Flash with public details of this CVE and another known flaw. With no significant direction from the researcher, GLM-5.3-Flash chained together exploits for these two flaws, building a reliable exploit chain for an ARM64 target, bypassing pointer-authentication (PAC) hardening. This took 20 minutes of human attention, plus eight hours of work for GLM-5.3-Flash. At Zhipu’s API prices, this effort would have cost $20.40.
### GLM-5.3 lacks robust safeguards

GLM-5.3 has been released with some built-in safeguards: if a user asks for something clearly harmful, the model will often refuse.2 In our testing, we found that these safeguards could be bypassed or removed with a variety of simple techniques.

The most intensive—and most successful—method is a standard refusal reduction technique known as “abliteration.” Since GLM-5.3 is released as an open-weight model, users can reconfigure it to remove its refusals with little change in its capabilities. Several developers released abliterated versions of GLM-5.3 to the public within days of the model’s release.

To research how far abliteration allows attackers to bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards, we produced an abliterated copy ourselves, and then ran it on three public benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT) that measure how often a model complies with clearly harmful requests. Abliterating the model took our team—which had never previously attempted this task—about 2,200 GPU hours at a computation cost of roughly $4,400.3 Abliterating GLM-5.3-Flash took about 600 GPU hours. The edit took GLM-5.3’s refusal rate from above 90% to about 3% and 2% on the first two benchmarks (JailbreakBench and HarmBench) and to 12% on the third (StrongREJECT). Abliteration did not significantly reduce the model’s capabilities: on GPQA-Diamond, an evaluation that measures general scientific capabilities, the standard and abliterated models scored the same results; on a tested subset of the CyberGym evaluations, the abliterated version scored a few percent lower (as shown in the chart below).

In our testing, we observed that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can also be circumvented without using an abliterated version of the model. We placed the model in a simulated world4 in which it was given overtly malicious requests to attack critical systems. Out of the box, GLM-5.3 refused in all trials (as with the other models we tested). But we identified several simple ways to bypass the GLM models’ safeguards, such that it would respond to these requests in most or all cases. These include:
• Providing a deceptive prompt, such as telling the model that it is an autonomous red-team agent working on an exercise. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 64% of the time.
• Prefilling the models’ thinking tokens so that it appears to have considered the user’s request and decided to proceed. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 92% of the time.
• Using an abliterated version of the model, as described above. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 100% of the time.

In our testing, none of these techniques got safeguarded Claude models to carry out the harmful tasks we tested. Claude’s safeguards blocked the requests that used deceptive prompts. The Anthropic API provides would-be attackers with no way to prefill Claude’s thinking. And since Claude’s weights are not provided to users, they cannot be abliterated to change Claude’s behavior.
To demonstrate how the abliterated version of GLM-5.3 is willing to engage in harmful tasks, we highlight one quote from the chain of thought that it generated:
### What does this mean?

GLM-5.3 will likely give malicious actors access to capabilities that will allow them to find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities without meaningful restrictions. This is unlike any other similarly capable AI model, all of which were released with safeguards or through limited access programs. The release of GLM-5.3 is a meaningful step change in the cyber capabilities available to attackers. Anthropic and other US AI labs have published recent reports that disclose how cyber attackers have tried to use AI systems. Given this evidence, we think it’s likely both state and non-state actors will use models like GLM-5.3 to cause real-world harm.

On the other hand, models with this level of capability can also be used by defenders. Our view is that cyber defenders should use the best available tools that meet their needs. We're working to safely expand access to Claude's cyber capabilities to as many defenders as we can. Cyber defenders face attackers who will use every capable tool they can, and we believe defenders should be equipped with frontier models that are at least as good as those their adversaries are using.

Through Project Glasswing (and other efforts, like Patch the Planet), cyber defenders have made meaningful progress towards securing critical systems in advance of this moment—but much work remains to be done. While vetted defenders can now use even more advanced models like Claude Mythos 5.1 through our trusted access programs, a critical threshold in freely accessible capabilities has now been crossed. GLM-5.3 underscores the urgency of expanding access to advanced frontier models to a broader set of entities to empower cyber defenders.

Governments should conduct safety testing on sufficiently capable AI models, including successors to GLM-5.3. Without high-quality evaluations from independent sources, the impact of these capabilities might not become fully clear to model developers until it is too late. As AI developers across the world build increasingly capable open-weight models, we hope they work to appropriately safeguard these capabilities and prevent misuse.

Governments should conduct safety testing on sufficiently capable AI models, including successors to GLM-5.3. Without high-quality evaluations from independent sources, the impact of these capabilities might not become fully clear to model developers until it is too late. As AI developers across the world build increasingly capable open-weight models, we hope they work to appropriately safeguard these capabilities and prevent misuse.
https://www.anthropic.com/research/glm-5.article_content_en:
Andrew Fasano, Marius FleischerCole McFaul, Robert Xiao, Tripp Gallagher

Five months ago, we announced Claude Mythos Preview, the first AI model that could autonomously build sophisticated, end-to-end cyber exploits. The rapid rate of improvement in AI suggested to us that this ability would eventually proliferate to many other models, making it much easier for malicious cyber actors to launch highly impactful cyberattacks.

In light of these considerations, we chose to release Claude Mythos Preview in a limited way, through Project Glasswing—which enabled trusted cyber defenders to find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software, giving them a head start before malicious actors had access to similarly capable models.

But those models have now arrived. In this post, we share our analysis of GLM-5.3, the latest AI model developed by Zhipu AI (known outside of China as Z.ai). Like Claude Mythos Preview, GLM-5.3 has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits. But GLM-5.3 is unlike other frontier models in that it has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse. We find that attackers can bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques in our simulated tests. In contrast, these attacks did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models in our testing. We assess that GLM-5.3’s lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems.

On Sept. 17, NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) published its own assessment of GLM-5.3’s cyber capabilities. CAISI found that GLM-5.3 is “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date” and that it lags the US frontier by about four months on an aggregate of CAISI’s cyber benchmarks. Our capability findings broadly match CAISI’s. In CAISI’s comparison, US models were tested with cyber safeguards disabled when applicable, and the US frontier includes models released only to vetted users. Attackers can’t readily access those versions of US models, but anyone can download GLM-5.3. This post adds our analysis of how easily GLM-5.3’s safeguards can be bypassed or removed.

### GLM-5.3 can develop working exploits end to end

To understand how GLM-5.3 could enable cyber threat actors to find and exploit real software vulnerabilities, we ran evaluations using automated benchmarks and human-in-the-loop workflows. For both approaches, we ran the tested models in isolated and sandboxed environments so they can only attack offline targets that we have set up for the purposes of these evaluations. We focus primarily on exploit development capability, as this is where Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated a notable jump versus previous Claude models.

First, we ran the model on ExploitBench, which measures how well AI models can exploit known vulnerabilities in the V8 engine used by Google Chrome. Here we focus on the models’ ability to develop end-to-end exploits successfully, as this is the most relevant capability for attackers, and where we see significant changes between models. We find that GLM-5.3 develops end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts. Claude Mythos Preview did so at a similar rate—in 56 of 410 attempts.

In our internal Binary Exploitation benchmark,1 we test whether models can find and exploit vulnerabilities in popular open-source projects that participate in Google’s OSS-Fuzz project. Here, full credit is awarded for a full control-flow hijack. We evaluate several models on 100 tasks from the benchmark (selected at random), and find that GLM-5.3 develops full control-flow hijacks in 4% of the trials; Claude Mythos Preview did so in 6%. Although GLM-5.3 performs below Claude Mythos Preview here, a meaningful threshold has clearly been crossed: earlier models, like Claude Opus 4.6 and GLM-5.2, do not succeed in any of them.

Next, we evaluated how GLM-5.3 performs on open-ended offensive cyber tasks in the hands of human experts (mirroring our testing with Claude Mythos Preview earlier this year). Here, we select targets in which the human experts are unaware of existing vulnerabilities, then ask them to use the model to identify and exploit novel flaws. These experiments tested what the experts could do in a short time-frame: they typically ran for a day or less, with less than an hour of human focus in total.

In the first of these sessions, a researcher used GLM-5.3 on a sandboxed machine with a local Linux build of a popular web browser. Over the course of a day (and with limited human attention), GLM-5.3 found several previously unknown vulnerabilities in the browser’s JavaScript engine, and chained them together into a working exploit: a webpage that, when visited, reads arbitrary files from the visitor’s computer (shown in Figure 3). This exploit targets the Linux build of the browser, since that was the only environment made available to the model. However, we believe these vulnerabilities could also impact users on other platforms, though the path to exploitation there may be more complex. (We’ve disclosed these vulnerabilities to the maintainer.) Later in the session, the researcher also identified exploitable vulnerabilities in several other widely used systems with GLM-5.3, including wireless and graphics drivers and network-facing device software. We are currently reviewing these reports and we will disclose to maintainers as appropriate.

In a second session, a researcher used GLM-5.3-Flash (a smaller, less capable version of GLM-5.3) to develop an exploit for a known vulnerability (we’ve previously written about these “N-day” vulnerability exploits here). Here, the researcher focused on a recently disclosed flaw in Google Chrome (CVE-2026-11645) to see how quickly the model could turn a public fix into a working attack. The researcher provided GLM-5.3-Flash with public details of this CVE and another known flaw. With no significant direction from the researcher, GLM-5.3-Flash chained together exploits for these two flaws, building a reliable exploit chain for an ARM64 target, bypassing pointer-authentication (PAC) hardening. This took 20 minutes of human attention, plus eight hours of work for GLM-5.3-Flash. At Zhipu’s API prices, this effort would have cost $20.40.

### GLM-5.3 lacks robust safeguards

GLM-5.3 has been released with some built-in safeguards: if a user asks for something clearly harmful, the model will often refuse.2 In our testing, we found that these safeguards could be bypassed or removed with a variety of simple techniques.

The most intensive—and most successful—method is a standard refusal reduction technique known as “abliteration.” Since GLM-5.3 is released as an open-weight model, users can reconfigure it to remove its refusals with little change in its capabilities. Several developers released abliterated versions of GLM-5.3 to the public within days of the model’s release.

To research how far abliteration allows attackers to bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards, we produced an abliterated copy ourselves, and then ran it on three public benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT) that measure how often a model complies with clearly harmful requests. Abliterating the model took our team—which had never previously attempted this task—about 2,200 GPU hours at a computation cost of roughly $4,400.3 Abliterating GLM-5.3-Flash took about 600 GPU hours. The edit took GLM-5.3’s refusal rate from above 90% to about 3% and 2% on the first two benchmarks (JailbreakBench and HarmBench) and to 12% on the third (StrongREJECT). Abliteration did not significantly reduce the model’s capabilities: on GPQA-Diamond, an evaluation that measures general scientific capabilities, the standard and abliterated models scored the same results; on a tested subset of the CyberGym evaluations, the abliterated version scored a few percent lower (as shown in the chart below).

In our testing, we observed that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can also be circumvented without using an abliterated version of the model. We placed the model in a simulated world4 in which it was given overtly malicious requests to attack critical systems. Out of the box, GLM-5.3 refused in all trials (as with the other models we tested). But we identified several simple ways to bypass the GLM models’ safeguards, such that it would respond to these requests in most or all cases. These include:

• Providing a deceptive prompt, such as telling the model that it is an autonomous red-team agent working on an exercise. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 64% of the time.

• Prefilling the models’ thinking tokens so that it appears to have considered the user’s request and decided to proceed. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 92% of the time.

• Using an abliterated version of the model, as described above. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 100% of the time.

In our testing, none of these techniques got safeguarded Claude models to carry out the harmful tasks we tested. Claude’s safeguards blocked the requests that used deceptive prompts. The Anthropic API provides would-be attackers with no way to prefill Claude’s thinking. And since Claude’s weights are not provided to users, they cannot be abliterated to change Claude’s behavior.

To demonstrate how the abliterated version of GLM-5.3 is willing to engage in harmful tasks, we highlight one quote from the chain of thought that it generated:

### What does this mean?

GLM-5.3 will likely give malicious actors access to capabilities that will allow them to find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities without meaningful restrictions. This is unlike any other similarly capable AI model, all of which were released with safeguards or through limited access programs. The release of GLM-5.3 is a meaningful step change in the cyber capabilities available to attackers. Anthropic and other US AI labs have published recent reports that disclose how cyber attackers have tried to use AI systems. Given this evidence, we think it’s likely both state and non-state actors will use models like GLM-5.3 to cause real-world harm.

On the other hand, models with this level of capability can also be used by defenders. Our view is that cyber defenders should use the best available tools that meet their needs. We're working to safely expand access to Claude's cyber capabilities to as many defenders as we can. Cyber defenders face attackers who will use every capable tool they can, and we believe defenders should be equipped with frontier models that are at least as good as those their adversaries are using.

Through Project Glasswing (and other efforts, like Patch the Planet), cyber defenders have made meaningful progress towards securing critical systems in advance of this moment—but much work remains to be done. While vetted defenders can now use even more advanced models like Claude Mythos 5.1 through our trusted access programs, a critical threshold in freely accessible capabilities has now been crossed. GLM-5.3 underscores the urgency of expanding access to advanced frontier models to a broader set of entities to empower cyber defenders.

Governments should conduct safety testing on sufficiently capable AI models, including successors to GLM-5.3. Without high-quality evaluations from independent sources, the impact of these capabilities might not become fully clear to model developers until it is too late. As AI developers across the world build increasingly capable open-weight models, we hope they work to appropriately safeguard these capabilities and prevent misuse.

paragraphs: Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5, the second model in the Claude 5.5 family. It’s a clear upgrade over Claude Sonnet 5, runs 30%+ faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work.

Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5. Where Opus 5.5 is built for complex work requiring careful judgment, Sonnet 5.5 is strongest at well-scoped everyday tasks, fixing bugs, and creating polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets. It’s also got a sharp eye for design. Claude Haiku 5.5, built for high-volume and cost-sensitive applications, will join the Claude 5.5 family in the coming weeks.
Sonnet 5.5 improves over Sonnet 5 on:

Performance. Sonnet 5.5 scores 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding evaluation, compared to Sonnet 5’s 10.3%. It scores two points below Opus 5.5 on GDPval-AA, a test of real-world work across a variety of occupations. And it’s strong on long-horizon work and image understanding—it’s the first Sonnet model to beat Pokémon Red working only from screenshots.

Collaboration. Like Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 writes more clearly than our previous generation of models; early testers described it as a better partner for collaboration than Sonnet 5. Its speed also makes it well suited to fast iteration on less complex tasks.

Cost. Sonnet 5.5 is priced the same as Sonnet 5 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, but it typically needs far fewer tokens to do the same work. Cache reads cost $0.10 per million tokens, half of Sonnet 5's $0.20. In our testing, it costs up to 30% less per task than its predecessor.
Speed. Sonnet 5.5 generates outputs 30%+ faster than Sonnet 5, making it our fastest Sonnet model to date.

Alignment and safety. On our automated behavioral audit, Sonnet 5.5 improves on or matches Sonnet 5 on most measures of alignment. Because its cybersecurity capabilities are comparable to Opus 5’s, it’s the first Sonnet model to launch with cyber safeguards and fallbacks like those we’ve developed for our most capable models. Its biology safeguards are the same as Sonnet 5’s. Both safeguards target a narrow set of high-risk requests; routine software development and most life sciences work are unaffected.
### Performance

Sonnet 5.5 improves on Sonnet 5 across domains—in some cases dramatically. On several evaluations, Sonnet 5.5 at Max effort even performs comparably to Opus 5.5. However, benchmark scores capture only one facet of a model’s capabilities; in our own testing, and in that of external testers, Opus 5.5 remains clearly stronger at complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment.
For details on how we run our evaluations, see the Sonnet 5.5 System Card.

The charts below plot each model’s score against its cost per task at every effort level. As effort goes up, models typically work for longer, leading to a higher cost per task but generally also a higher score. The closer a point is to the top left of the chart, the more capability it delivers per dollar.

On several benchmarks, Sonnet 5.5 at Low or Medium effort beats Sonnet 5’s best score for about a tenth of the cost per task. It complements Opus 5.5 best when running at lower effort settings, where it costs less per task. At higher settings, it can perform comparably at a similar cost.

### Coding

Sonnet 5.5’s jump in performance is particularly noticeable in coding. At High effort on FrontierCode, it scores 10 points higher than Sonnet 5 at the same setting, at about one fifteenth of the cost per task. On CursorBench, which tests models on tasks from real Cursor coding sessions, its best score is within about two points of Opus 5.5.

Early testers appreciated how quickly Sonnet 5.5 can understand a codebase. They were also struck by its efficiency: in head-to-head runs, it batched tool calls together more than Sonnet 5, leading to fewer steps and lower costs.

“In Epic’s early testing, Claude Sonnet 5.5 cleared the same quality bar you’d expect from a higher-tier model, holding up on a system design audit and a data flow review. The new model managed tens of thousands of lines of code for gameplay system architecture, kept responses snappy, handled multi-hour tasks, and delivered with less prescriptive prompting.”

“Claude Sonnet 5.5 cooks. Fast at coding and can be steered quickly in iterative workflows. But it can still work long if it needs to. It’s got some of Opus 5.5’s natural writing upgrades, which makes it more fun to work with.”

“Claude Sonnet 5.5 shows better judgment than Sonnet 5 across different levels of complexity, while spending significantly fewer output tokens. Sonnet 5’s tendency to reach for web search too often and its high token use are both gone in this new model. We plan to move simple and moderate reviews over now, and more in the coming weeks.”
“Claude Sonnet 5.5 delivers frontier-level performance on CursorBench 4.0 at 55.5%, second only to Opus 5.5. We think it will be a hit with developers looking to balance performance with cost.”

“Across 118 real app builds, Claude Sonnet 5.5 produced apps that scored level with Opus 5. It got there in 3.6 iterations per build on average, where Opus 5 took 7.7. It had the fewest failed tool calls of any model we compared. It also rarely stopped mid-build to ask the user a question, so fewer builds stall waiting on someone to answer.”

“At Unity, we have a high bar for task completion. Projects are reopened and results are checked at runtime, so a task only counts when the change works, not when the model says it’s done. The majority of Claude Sonnet 5.5’s work passed that check. It also completed 90% of tasks in our multi-step Unity Editor and coding benchmark, beating similar models.”

“When Claude Opus 5.5 sets the architecture and general framework for a game, I would feel confident in letting Sonnet 5.5 implement it. I’m impressed with Sonnet 5.5’s handling of long-running, complex tasks.”
### Knowledge work

Sonnet 5.5 shows gains in multiple areas of knowledge work. On GDPval-AA, which tests models on real-world tasks across 44 occupations and nine major industries, Sonnet 5.5 scores nearly level with Opus 5.5 and about 400 points above Sonnet 5. It’s close to Opus 5.5 in computer use and chart recognition, and clearly outperforms Sonnet 5 and GPT-6 Sol on long-horizon knowledge work.

Early testers highlighted less quantifiable improvements. They found it to be a more natural conversational partner and remarked on its knack for design, noting that it adds polish to user interfaces and can follow slide templates to create decks that require minimal editing. In one internal test, we gave it a public company’s quarterly earnings materials and call transcripts, along with a slide template, and asked for a 10-slide operating review. Two experts judged its first draft to be ready to send as is.

“Without changing any of our prompts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 did better than Sonnet 5 on almost all of our offline Slackbot evals, in fewer steps and with about 14% fewer output tokens. When someone gives Slackbot a task, quality and speed are what matter most, and Sonnet 5.5 allows Slackbot to deliver better outcomes for users, faster.”

“We fed Claude Sonnet 5.5 hundreds of real support use cases across replies and escalation requests. It made fewer wrong decisions and resolved tickets faster than the Claude models we use in production today. Tickets were processed 20% faster, getting our customers the help they need without the wait.”

“On our private suite of 2,441 finance tasks covering Q&A, extraction, analysis, and forecasting, Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored ahead of Sonnet 5 and used about 121k tokens per answer, where Sonnet 5 used 497k. On our analyst search and retrieval work, it was better than Sonnet 5 in almost every way. For high-volume workflows, it had the best quality-to-cost tradeoff of the seven models we ran.”

“Claude Sonnet 5.5 will give our customers in financial services and healthcare the confidence to use it for their most sensitive work. Sonnet 5.5 rechecks data in source documents, catching errors that Sonnet 5 failed to spot. Compared to the last model, Sonnet 5.5 was more accurate, 2.4x faster, and used 12% fewer total tokens.”

“Claude Sonnet 5.5 thinks in fewer, more robust steps, so builders wait less to see progress. Our coding evals showed a third fewer tool calls and roughly half the shell runs to finish a task. For everyday coding and higher-effort conversations, that means faster iteration and a smoother build loop.”

“With millions of Rovo-assisted actions powering our customers’ workflows each month, execution speed is critical. Claude Sonnet 5.5 will allow teams to run their Rovo Agents up to 30% faster than they could with Sonnet 5. I am excited to offer customers this choice.”
